title: APL\360 on a 3D IBM 2741
summary: Throwback Thursday: A'70, APL\360 printing on green-bar paper at an IBM 2741's own pace, in 3D on a model from console-3D, on the way to a virtual computer history museum.

scenes.heading: APL\360 on a 3D IBM 2741
lines: A'70: APL\360 as it was typed in 1970

scenes.heading: Sharpening the saw
scenes.narration: This is my first narrated video in a while. I've been sharpening my saw, to make videos with higher production value, more quickly, using Remotion. I have a lot of topics waiting, in machine learning, computer history, and new programming languages. This one is computer history.

scenes.heading: My first program
scenes.narration: My first program was a horse race, written in {APL|A P L}, and typed on an {IBM|I B M} {2741|twenty-seven forty-one}, in nineteen seventy-two. Now that terminal is back, as a {3D|three D} model, running my clean-room {APL|A P L} three sixty in the browser.

items.sub: Kenneth Iverson's notation for describing algorithms
Iverson, Adin Falkoff and a small group at IBM Research
typed on an IBM 2741, with the APL type element

scenes.heading: The IBM 2741
scenes.narration: The {2741|twenty-seven forty-one} was a Selectric typewriter, turned into a terminal. With an {APL|A P L} type element in it, it was how most people met {APL|A P L} three sixty, in the late nineteen sixties and early seventies. You typed a line, the keyboard locked, and the answer came back on the same paper, at about fifteen characters a second.

scenes.heading: The type element
scenes.narration: The type element spun and tilted to each character. {APL|A P L}'s special symbols were on that element. The ones that weren't were made by overstriking, one character, a backspace, and another on top of it.

scenes.heading: At the 2741's own pace
scenes.narration: My demo, called A seventy, now prints the same way. What the session prints goes to the paper one character at a time, at about fifteen characters a second, with a little jitter. A carriage return takes longer, the farther the carriage has to travel. And the keyboard stays locked until printing finishes, as it did then.

scenes.heading: Green-bar paper
scenes.narration: The paper is continuous green-bar, fan-fold, with stripes three lines deep, and a sprocket hole every half inch down both edges. It runs from the platen, up past the top, then over and down behind, with a perforation every sixty-six lines.

scenes.heading: My model of the 2741
scenes.narration: The terminal is my model of the {2741|twenty-seven forty-one}, from {console|console} three D, my set of {3D|three D} models of historical consoles and terminals. It's built in Blender, and drawn in the browser with three J S. As the session prints, the carrier moves to each column, and back at the return, and the type element tilts and turns to each character.

scenes.heading: Three views, and 2D
scenes.narration: There are three views. The nearest is for reading as you type, and it's the default. The half view shows the keyboard, with its {APL|A P L} symbols. The third shows the entire machine. And a two D button switches back to the flat paper.

scenes.heading: A longer session: Life
scenes.narration: Here is a longer session. Load the Life workspace from library one, and describe it. List the function that makes each generation, Conway's Game of Life, in two lines. Then run it, for two generations of a glider.

scenes.heading: Recorded sound
scenes.narration: The sound is recorded, not synthesized. A key strike, pitched a little by its character, the space bar, and a thud at the return. Each visit opens on a card that starts the session with sound, or silently.

items.sub: Python, written by the X_eTaL program, with construction helpers
A'70 in the browser: the carrier and type element move

scenes.heading: console-3D
scenes.narration: The {2741|twenty-seven forty-one} is one of nine models in {console|console} three D. The {IBM|I B M} {1053|ten fifty-three} {console|console} printer, from the {1130|eleven thirty} and {1800|eighteen hundred}. The {5471|fifty-four seventy-one} printer keyboard, from System three. The Radio Shack {TRS-80|T R S eighty}. An {IBM|I B M} {PC|P C}, with two monitors. The {IBM|I B M} {3279|thirty-two seventy-nine} graphics terminal. The {029|oh twenty-nine} keypunch. My {COR24|core twenty-four} development board. And a MacBook Pro.

scenes.heading: APL, and my demos of it
The APL timeline
scenes.narration: A seventy is the first stop on my {APL|A P L} timeline, which opens on nineteen seventy. The other working demos are B seventy-five, {APL|A P L} on the {IBM|I B M} fifty-one hundred, and C eighty, on the {TRS-80|T R S eighty}. And D eighty-three is {IBM|I B M} {PC|P C} {APL|A P L}.

scenes.heading: A virtual computer history museum
scenes.narration: This is part of my ongoing work, to build a virtual computer history museum. It covers the languages {APL|A P L}, Lisp, and Forth, and also assemblers. And it covers machines like the {IBM|I B M} {1130|eleven thirty} and {1800|eighteen hundred}. Also the {UNIVAC|Univac} eleven ten, the {RCA|R C A} eighteen oh two, and the {IBM|I B M} three sixty. Still to do for {APL|A P L} is keypunching University of Maryland {APL|A P L}. Then {APL|A P L} eleven thirty on the ten fifty-three {console|console} printer, and {APL|A P L} two on a thirty-two seventy-nine G color terminal.

scenes.heading: Try it
scenes.narration: Try it yourself. Open A seventy, choose start with sound, and type a line, say, two three reshape iota six, or plus reduce iota one hundred. The links are in the description.
